name: When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
authors: Ryo Kamoi, Yusen Zhang, Nan Zhang, Jiawei Han, Rui Zhang (Penn State University; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign). First author Ryo Kamoi et al.
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), Volume 12, pp. 1417-1440, MIT Press, 2024 (arXiv 2406.01297, June 2024)
code_url: No executable code (this is a survey). Author maintains a companion paper list: https://github.com/ryokamoi/llm-self-correction-papers
reflection_type: none (analysis/survey). The survey itself proposes no new method; it categorizes and critically analyzes verbal-self-critique (intrinsic self-correction), tool-verified self-correction, and fine-tuned/learned-critic self-correction across the surveyed literature.
feedback_source: n/a as a method. As an analysis, it categorizes feedback sources used by surveyed work: self-generated (prompted LLM self-evaluation), external-tool (code interpreter, search engine, proof assistant, Wikipedia API), ground-truth-oracle (unrealistic settings), human assessment, and fine-tuned feedback/critic models. Its central finding is that the feedback-generation stage is the bottleneck.
iteration_structure: n/a (survey). It frames self-correction as a 3-stage pipeline (initial response generation -> feedback -> refinement), typically iterative-refine in the surveyed methods, but proposes no iteration scheme of its own.
reflection_object: Survey analysis, not a method. The object of self-correction in the surveyed literature is the LLM's output content / response (e.g., refining a generated answer, code, or text), optionally via reflecting on the reasoning chain. The survey's own 'object' is the research-question taxonomy and experimental methodology of the self-correction field, plus model weights when discussing fine-tuning-based self-correction.
learning_locus: n/a (analysis/survey). The survey spans both in_context_verbal (intrinsic/prompted self-correction) and gradient_weight_update (fine-tuning-enabled self-correction) paradigms; it concludes intrinsic in-context self-correction is unreliable in general tasks while large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction.
requires_training: n/a (survey). It analyzes methods spanning none (prompted intrinsic), SFT (large-scale fine-tuning on reference feedback, e.g., SelFee, Self-Critique, Baldur), RL (RL4F, and emerging o1-style RL post-survey), and cross-model critic training (REFINER, RL4F). Key finding: large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction.
reward_or_critic_model: n/a (survey). Categorizes the improvement signals used by surveyed work: self-as-judge (prompted LLM, found unreliable), trained reward/critic model (cross-model: REFINER T5, RL4F T5, Self-Correction GPT-Neo), verifiable reward / reliable external feedback (code interpreter, proof assistant), and unrealistic ground-truth oracle.
distillation_target: n/a as a method. In the surveyed fine-tuning line, reflection/feedback is distilled into model-weights (large-scale fine-tuning on reference feedback); the survey identifies this as the main reliable route besides external tools.
emergent_vs_engineered: Survey covers both. It primarily analyzes prompt/scaffold-engineered self-correction (e.g., Self-Refine, Reflexion, RCI, CRITIC) and finds it unreliable; in Section 12 it notes the emerging RL-trained/emergent reflection trend (OpenAI o1, Kumar et al. 2024, Qu et al. 2024) as a promising post-survey direction.
memory_type: n/a (survey). Surveyed intrinsic methods mostly use short-term/scratchpad-style within-pass refinement; some (e.g., Reflexion) use episodic memory of past attempts, but the survey itself proposes no memory mechanism.
memory_persistence: n/a (survey). Surveyed methods range from within-episode refinement to cross-episode retry memory (Reflexion); not a property of the survey itself.
error_localization_granularity: Survey analysis. It discusses self-correction mostly at the response/outcome level, and highlights that decomposable responses (where verification can be done per-component / step-level) are exceptionally suited to self-correction; recognizing errors is only easier than generating answers for tasks whose verification is exceptionally easy.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: Primarily intra-task: the survey defines self-correction as inference-time refinement of a response within a single task (initial response -> feedback -> refinement). It explicitly scopes out broader self-training/self-improvement that transfers across tasks (Section 9 distinguishes it from Pan et al. 2024).
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: post-hoc-revision. The survey's notion of self-correction is post-hoc refinement of an initial response (mid-inference), not mid-trajectory recovery or next-episode avoidance.
task_domains: Survey spans: reasoning/math, code, closed-book knowledge QA, open-book/context-based QA, open-ended text generation (dialogue, summarization, detoxification), decision-making/planning (computer tasks, games), and general alignment. Findings differ by domain: external-tool tasks (code) work well; general reasoning/knowledge intrinsic self-correction does not.
benchmarks: Aggregated across surveyed papers: GSM8K, SVAMP, MATH-style math reasoning, HumanEval/MBPP-style and text-to-code coding, HotpotQA, CommonsenseQA (CSQA), Natural Questions (NQ), Strategy/SQA, QReCC, MiniWoB++/computer tasks, ALFWorld-style game environments, MT-Bench, topic-based summarization, detoxification (RealToxicityPrompts-style), proof generation (Baldur). No single benchmark is the survey's own.
headline_result: Three headline conclusions (qualitative meta-findings, not a single number): (1) no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except in tasks exceptionally suited for it; (2) self-correction works well in tasks with reliable external feedback (e.g., code via interpreters); (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction. The bottleneck is feedback generation, not refinement.
baselines: Methodological critique: the survey argues many self-correction studies are not compared against sufficiently strong baselines (RQ3). It re-categorizes prior frameworks as Realistic (Fair / Unfair) vs Unrealistic (oracle), exposing over-evaluation. It compares against negative-results papers (Huang et al. 2024a 'LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet'; CRITIC-without-tool; RCI without oracle).
gains_vs_baseline: No own quantitative delta (survey). Its comparative finding: intrinsic prompted self-correction shows no reliable net gain over best-possible initial responses in general tasks; reported gains in prior work often stem from weak initial-response prompts (unfair) or oracle stopping/feedback (unrealistic), which over-evaluate self-correction.
compute_cost_profile: Survey notes self-correction adds inference-time cost (extra generation + feedback + refinement passes, i.e., a multiplier over single-pass generation) and that fine-tuning-based self-correction requires large-scale human-annotated training data; it argues this cost is often not justified versus stronger single-pass baselines (RQ3 under-examined).
known_limitations: (1) LLMs struggle to generate reliable feedback on their own responses via in-context learning (feedback-generation bottleneck). (2) Many prior studies do not define research questions precisely (conflate RQ1/RQ2/RQ3). (3) Common over-evaluation via oracle information (ground-truth stop/feedback = unrealistic) and weak initial-response prompts (unfair). (4) Survey scope: inference-time self-correction only, primarily papers up to May 2024; cross-model setups cannot test RQ1/RQ2.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: THE central thesis: self-correction's success is determined by the feedback source. intrinsic-only (prompted self-verify) generally fails in general tasks; external-tool/verifier (reliable feedback, e.g., code interpreter, proof assistant, search-derived info) works; oracle-label/ground-truth settings are unrealistic and over-evaluate; fine-tuned feedback (env/reward-trained) works at scale. Reliable external feedback or large-scale fine-tuning is required.
self_correction_efficacy: task-dependent / requires-oracle-or-external-feedback. Net-positive only when (a) the task is exceptionally suited (decomposable / verification much easier than generation), (b) reliable external feedback is available, or (c) large-scale fine-tuning is used. Intrinsic prompted self-correction is not shown to be net-positive in general tasks without label leakage.
calibration_effect: not-measured (survey predates the reasoning-model 'reasoning tax' framing). It documents that prompted LLMs frequently fail to detect their own mistakes (poor self-verification), implying weak self-assessment, but does not quantify a calibration/overconfidence effect.
failure_attribution_capability: classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy). It provides a taxonomy of self-correction research questions (RQ1/RQ2/RQ3) and frameworks (Realistic: Fair/Unfair vs Unrealistic/oracle), and catalogs failure/over-evaluation modes in prior work (oracle stopping, oracle feedback, weak initial-response prompts, insufficient baselines, conflated RQs).
failure_mode_addressed: Targets methodological/evaluation failure modes of the self-correction literature: superficial/unreliable self-reflection (LLMs cannot generate good feedback on their own outputs), over-evaluation via oracle information, unfair weak initial-response prompts, conflation of distinct research questions, and missing strong baselines. It exposes 'self-correction does not actually work intrinsically' as the core illusory result.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: No new dataset/benchmark. Releases a checklist for designing appropriate self-correction experiments (Section 8) and a companion curated paper list (github.com/ryokamoi/llm-self-correction-papers) as reusable community resources.
builds_on: Motivated by negative-results analyses, esp. Huang et al. 2024a 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet' (ICLR 2024). Complements Pan et al. 2024 survey on self-correction (broader, includes training). Surveys foundational methods: Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), RCI (Kim et al. 2023), CRITIC (Gou et al. 2024), Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022), Self-Debug, RARR, SelFee, Baldur, REFINER, RL4F, Self-Correction (Welleck et al. 2023).
extended_by_or_inspired: Frequently cited as the authoritative critical reference on when LLM self-correction works; cited by subsequent self-correction / self-verification analyses (e.g., 'Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction') and by RL-trained self-correction work (SCoRe/Kumar et al. 2024, Qu et al. 2024) and o1-style reasoning-model discussions. The same group's 'Evaluating LLMs at Detecting Errors in LLM Responses' (COLM 2024) is a closely related follow-up.
citation_count: 288 (Google Scholar, as of 2026-06; confirmed via Ryo Kamoi's verified Scholar profile)
reasoning_model_native: Partially. The survey predates wide reasoning-model deployment but Section 12 explicitly discusses OpenAI o1 (RL-trained to recognize and refine its own mistakes) and RL-based self-correction (Kumar et al. 2024, Qu et al. 2024) as the emerging trend; it does not yet hold conclusions specific to o1/R1-class models, noting they are not comprehensively analyzed.
on_policy_distillation_link: Indirect. The survey's finding that large-scale fine-tuning (SFT on reference feedback) and RL/self-corrective learning (Welleck et al. 2023) are the reliable routes to self-correction connects to distilling correction ability into weights; it does not discuss on-policy distillation by name.
sample_efficiency: Not applicable as a single number (survey). It notes fine-tuning-based self-correction typically relies on large training data / large-scale human annotation and flags self-correction with small training data as an unexplored, sample-efficiency-relevant future direction.
